head.citation-title: Exploring CO2 mineralization for enhanced high-temperature exposure in cement-based materials containing slag cement and fly ash cenosphere
head.abstracts: © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.This study investigates the effectiveness of early-age CO2 curing (CC) in improving the post-fire performance of mortars incorporating slag cement (SC) and fly-ash cenospheres (FAC). Mortars were produced with ordinary portland cement (OPC) partially replaced with 25% and 50% SC or FAC at two water-to-cementitious materials (w/cm) ratios, using 100% OPC mixtures as reference. Specimens were exposed to CC at 20% CO2, while unexposed specimens served as the control. All samples were then water-cured for 28 days and subsequently exposed to temperature regimes of 23°C (room temperature), 200°C, 400°C, and 600°C. Compressive strength, transport properties, porosity quantification, and thermogravimetric analysis were conducted to evaluate the synergistic effect of CC, FAC and SC. Results show that CO₂ curing enhanced early-age compressive strength and refined the pore structure of OPC and slag mixes, particularly at 25–50% SC, while its effect on FAC mixes was limited due to low calcium content and high porosity. All mixtures gained strength at 200–400°C, with losses at 600°C; CC reduced strength loss in OPC and SC mixes by forming stable calcium carbonate, which decomposes at higher temperatures, improving residual performance. For example, 50S samples subjected to CC lost 24% of their strength, compared to 34% for the non-exposed samples. Slag replacement decreased water absorption, sorptivity, and void volume, producing denser matrices, whereas FAC increased porosity and transport properties, limiting strength but enhancing thermal stability due to its porous, low-conductivity structure. Overall, CO₂ curing refines pore size and connectivity, while binder type dominates microstructure and post-fire behavior.

coredata.dc:description: This study investigates the effectiveness of early-age CO2 curing (CC) in improving the post-fire performance of mortars incorporating slag cement (SC) and fly-ash cenospheres (FAC). Mortars were produced with ordinary portland cement (OPC) partially replaced with 25% and 50% SC or FAC at two water-to-cementitious materials (w/cm) ratios, using 100% OPC mixtures as reference. Specimens were exposed to CC at 20% CO2, while unexposed specimens served as the control. All samples were then water-cured for 28 days and subsequently exposed to temperature regimes of 23°C (room temperature), 200°C, 400°C, and 600°C. Compressive strength, transport properties, porosity quantification, and thermogravimetric analysis were conducted to evaluate the synergistic effect of CC, FAC and SC. Results show that CO₂ curing enhanced early-age compressive strength and refined the pore structure of OPC and slag mixes, particularly at 25–50% SC, while its effect on FAC mixes was limited due to low calcium content and high porosity. All mixtures gained strength at 200–400°C, with losses at 600°C; CC reduced strength loss in OPC and SC mixes by forming stable calcium carbonate, which decomposes at higher temperatures, improving residual performance. For example, 50S samples subjected to CC lost 24% of their strength, compared to 34% for the non-exposed samples. Slag replacement decreased water absorption, sorptivity, and void volume, producing denser matrices, whereas FAC increased porosity and transport properties, limiting strength but enhancing thermal stability due to its porous, low-conductivity structure. Overall, CO₂ curing refines pore size and connectivity, while binder type dominates microstructure and post-fire behavior.
